articles.title: In 2021, YouTubers MrBeast and Mark Rober set out to remove 30 million pounds of waterway rubbish; the campaign later removed 34 million pounds
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In a groundbreaking campaign, YouTubers MrBeast and Mark Rober launched #TeamSeas, successfully raising over $33 million to remove 34 million pounds of waste from oceans, rivers, and beaches, surpassing their initial goal. Find out how the community came together to tackle ocean pollution and support environmental initiatives.
articles.body: In October 2021, two of YouTube’s most prominent content creators set an uncommonly specific target to be achieved in a digital fundraising campaign: collect 30 million pounds of waste products from the Earth’s oceans, rivers and beaches, one pound for every dollar collected. Nearly three years after its launch, the fundraising phase of their campaign, known as #TeamSeas, concluded when Ocean Conservancy announced in July 2024 that the initiative had removed 34,080,191 pounds of trash from waters in 73 countries around the world.The campaign followed a tree-planting fundraiser that had already proven the model#TeamSeas is the follow-up project of Team Trees, which is the tree plantation initiative started by Jimmy Donaldson, aka MrBeast, along with Mark Rober, a former NASA engineer turned science YouTuber, in October 2019. The previous effort set out to raise $20 million to plant 20 million trees and met its tree‑planting goal, with the campaign now showing “25M+ trees funded and counting” and “800K+ donors worldwide”. Two years later, the duo used the same approach, but instead of trees and forests, they targeted plastic waste in the oceans. This time the organizations involved were Ocean Conservancy and The Ocean Cleanup.Every dollar pledged was tied to a pound of trashThe idea was straightforward and deliberately so: donate one dollar and one pound of trash would be removed as part of #TeamSeas. There was an established public goal for the campaign, which required reaching $30 million by January 1, 2022; the challenge was easily surpassed, with the whole $30 million raised in only 65 days by contributions from more than 400,000 people. Donations kept coming in after that milestone, and by the time the campaign wrapped in July 2024, the total had climbed to roughly $34 million, matching the one-pound-per-dollar pledge behind the final 34,080,191-pound tally.More than 8,000 creators helped push the campaign past a billion viewsWhat made # TeamSeas stand out was that it featured a huge number of content creators. According to YouTube's own announcement of the campaign, more than 8,000 creators from 145 countries pledged their support, with popular figures like Marques Brownlee, LinusTechTips, and Dhar Mann, among others, taking part. In total, video posts with the hashtag generated over 1.3 billion views. The money collected via #TeamSeas was split evenly between Ocean Conservancy and The Ocean Cleanup. Both organizations took a specific approach to addressing the problem that was present: Ocean Conservancy worked with beaches and the ocean, including removing ghost fishing gear, while The Ocean Cleanup focused on intercepting trash in rivers before it could reach the sea. Ocean Conservancy, which has run its International Coastal Cleanup every year since 1986, used its coordinator network and its Global Ghost Gear Initiative to carry out 1,962 coastal, underwater, and abandoned fishing gear cleanup projects with over 172,000 volunteers across 73 countries, from Haines, Alaska to Aldabra Atoll, Seychelles.The final total landed four million pounds past the original goalThe total weight of 34,080,191 pounds was confirmed in Ocean Conservancy's July 2024 announcement marking the campaign's conclusion, more than 4 million pounds past the original 30-million-pound goal. "It's awesome that the YouTube community came together to make it happen," #TeamSeas co-founder MrBeast said in the announcement.A 2020 paper in Science, “Evaluating scenarios toward zero plastic pollution”, by Lau and colleagues, modeled the flow of plastic waste into aquatic and terrestrial ecosystems. The researchers found that roughly 11 million metric tons of plastic enter the ocean every year, a figure they projected would nearly triple to about 29 million metric tons by 2040 without major changes to how plastic is produced and managed. Cleanups such as #TeamSeas do not tackle the flow directly, although they help eliminate any materials that have already entered the cycle before they get broken down further. The decomposition process is important; nevertheless, a January 2024 study led by Madeleine Milne of the University of Toronto and Dr. Britta Baechler of Ocean Conservancy, published in Environmental Pollution, found microplastic particles in 88 percent of protein food samples tested, including fish, beef, chicken, and several plant-based meat alternatives. Using separate survey data, the same research team estimated that an average adult in the United States consumes about 11,500 microplastic particles per year from protein alone, with some estimates running as high as 3.8 million.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Harvard University has a 'September message' for all international students planning to leave America as well as those staying in the country
articles.summary: Tech News News: Harvard University has issued a pointed advisory to its international student community, urging both those currently abroad and those already in the U.
articles.body: Harvard University has issued a pointed advisory to its international student community, urging both those currently abroad and those already in the United States to pay close attention to a looming deadline: September 15, when a major overhaul of F-1 and J-1 visa rules takes effect. On that date, new Department of Homeland Security rules will take effect, replacing the long‑standing “duration of status” system with fixed visa end dates. Students already in the U.S. before the deadline will retain current protections, while those re‑entering after September 15 will face stricter limits.What Harvard University is telling the international studentsThe Harvard International Office has recommended that F-1 students, J-1 exchange scholars, and anyone enrolled in on-campus programs this fall try to be physically present in the US before the new rule kicks in. The advisory is aimed squarely at students who might be traveling internationally around the deadline — including many from India and other countries — and urges them to review their visa documents, Form I-20 or DS-2019, and I-94 records, and to consult the university's international office before booking any travel.Harvard emphasised that the rule change won't stop newly admitted students from starting their programs this fall. The concern is narrower but significant: students who leave the country and re-enter on or after September 15 will be pulled into the new visa framework, potentially losing more favourable treatment they'd otherwise be entitled to simply by staying put.What's actually changingThe rule, finalised by the Department of Homeland Security and published in the Federal Register on July 17, 2026, eliminates the long-standing "duration of status" system that has allowed F-1 and J-1 visa holders to remain in the U.S. for as long as they maintain their academic or exchange program, without a fixed expiration date. In its place, the government will assign every F, J, and I visa holder a specific "Admit Until Date," generally tied to the length of their program as listed on their I-20 or DS-2019 form, capped at a maximum of four years regardless of how long the underlying program actually runs.Students already in the U.S. and maintaining valid status when the rule takes effect will generally be grandfathered into a transition period, allowed to stay until either their program's end date or the expiration of any post-completion work authorisation they qualify for, subject to that same four-year cap. Anyone who travels internationally and returns after September 15, however, will be issued a new fixed Admit Until Date upon re-entry, even if they had previously been in the country under the old open-ended system.The change also trims the standard F-1 grace period after finishing a program from 60 days down to 30, and adds new restrictions on switching majors or degree levels and on transferring laterally between graduate programs. Students in programs that naturally run longer than four years, including many doctoral candidates, will need to file formal extension requests with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services — a process that brings additional biometrics, background checks, and fees.The student visa overhaul lands alongside the State Department's routine September 2026 Visa Bulletin, which governs the pace at which immigrant visas move forward across family- and employment-based categories. While that bulletin doesn't directly affect F-1 or J-1 student status, it's a reminder of just how much the broader U.S. visa system is in flux this month — from student status rules to green card backlogs — for the many international students, including from countries like India and China, who may eventually seek to transition from a student visa to longer-term immigration status.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Google CEO Sundar Pichai’s IIT batchmate became a famous monk; what he told Pichai when they met years later: “You deal with Google, which creates stress. I deal with…”
articles.summary: US News: One went on to lead Google. The other chose a life of spirituality. Both were IIT graduates from the same year, but their careers took them in entirel.
articles.body: One went on to lead Google. The other chose a life of spirituality. Both were IIT graduates from the same year, but their careers took them in entirely different directions. Google CEO Sundar Pichai and ISKCON monk Gauranga Das were part of the 1993 IIT graduating batch. Pichai studied at IIT Kharagpur, while Das attended IIT Bombay. Years later, when the two met, a light-hearted exchange about their appearances turned into a memorable comparison between corporate life and spirituality.During an address at the India Global Forum (IGF) in London in June 2025, Das recalled Pichai telling him, “You look younger than me.” “You deal with Google, which creates stress. I deal with God, who releases stress,” he replied to the Google CEO. The remark became the most memorable part of their reunion story.Sundar Pichai: The IIT graduate who became Google CEOSundar Pichai’s journey from IIT Kharagpur to the top of Google is one of the most recognisable Indian-origin success stories in the technology industry. Pichai completed his BTech at IIT Kharagpur in 1993. He later moved to the US for higher studies, earning a master’s degree in materials science and engineering from Stanford University and an MBA from the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania.Pichai joined Google in 2004. He worked on products including Google Chrome and Chrome OS before taking on wider leadership responsibilities. He became CEO of Google in August 2015. In December 2019, he also became CEO of Alphabet, Google’s parent company.Gauranga Das: The IIT Bombay graduate who chose a spiritual lifeGauranga Das, also known as Gauranga Prabhu, followed a different route after graduating from IIT Bombay. According to a TOI report, Das was part of the same IIT batch as Pichai, although the two studied at different campuses and branches. While Pichai entered the technology industry, Das eventually left his corporate career and pursued spirituality. He became a monk and senior leader within the International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON).Das is also an author of books including The Art of Resilience and The Art of Focus. His work has included spiritual education, social initiatives and leadership programmes. His professional life is centred on spirituality, teaching and service.When Sundar Pichai met his IIT batchmate againThe story of the two IIT alumni became widely discussed after Gauranga Das spoke about their meeting at the India Global Forum 2025 in London. Das recalled that he and Pichai had been in the same IIT batch but had not interacted during college. They reportedly met years later, reportedly at Akash Ambani’s wedding in 2019. Das said that Pichai remarked on his youthful appearance. “Years later, we met, and he said, ‘You look younger than me.’ I replied, ‘You deal with Google, which creates stress. I deal with God, who releases stress,’” he said.The joke captured the difference between their careers.Two IIT alumni, two very different ideas of successPichai and Das share an academic connection, but their professional journeys are very different. Pichai pursued technology, worked his way up at Google and became the CEO of the company. Das chose spirituality, became an ISKCON monk and built a public career around teaching, writing and social work. Their story is not about one path being better than the other. It is about how two graduates from the same IIT batch can make very different choices about their lives.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2018, Microsoft sank 864 servers 117 feet beneath the North Sea to cool them naturally; two years later, their failure rate was one-eighth that of land-based machines
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Microsoft's underwater data center achieved a failure rate one-eighth that of land-based servers, leveraging seawater cooling and a sealed nitrogen environment as part of Project Natick.
articles.body: Microsoft lowered a sealed cylindrical data center that contained 864 servers into the North Sea off Scotland's Orkney Islands in 2018. The 40-foot-long vessel was placed about 117 feet below the surface as part of Project Natick, which was an experiment designed to test whether data centers could operate reliably on the seabed while using seawater as part of the cooling system.When Microsoft retrieved the vessel in 2020, the company found that the servers inside had experienced a failure rate one-eighth that of its land-based comparison group. Microsoft's own Project Natick results describe the reliability difference as one of the main findings from the experiment.A data center inside a steel vesselThe Northern Isles module contained 12 server racks that held 864 servers. InformationWeek reported that the cylindrical vessel was approximately 40 feet long and 10 feet wide and was installed at a depth of 117 feet. The sealed vessel was filled with nitrogen rather than ordinary air, which created an environment with less oxygen and therefore less potential for corrosion inside the enclosure.Cooling was one of the central engineering reasons for putting the equipment underwater. The system transferred heat to the surrounding seawater instead of relying on the same cooling infrastructure used by a conventional land-based facility, and the vessel was connected to land by cables that supplied power and provided the network connection. It was designed to operate without technicians entering the module to carry out routine maintenance.Two years without routine maintenanceMicrosoft retrieved the Northern Isles module in July 2020 and compared the performance of its servers with a group of land-based machines. The underwater servers had a failure rate one-eighth that of the land-based control group, to which Microsoft said the result suggested that the controlled environment inside the vessel had produced more reliable operation than conventional conditions.Microsoft's researchers proposed two main explanations for the difference, firstly, the nitrogen atmosphere inside the vessel was less corrosive than an oxygen-rich atmosphere, and secondly, the absence of people working around the equipment eliminated some of the physical disturbance that servers experience in conventional data centers. Microsoft's Project Natick research page says the company believed those factors were responsible for much of the reliability difference, although it also described the explanation as a hypothesis requiring further analysis.The project therefore tested whether a sealed data center could operate for long periods without the normal human access associated with land-based facilities. The experiment also used ordinary commercial server hardware rather than equipment created specifically for an underwater installation.The experiment ended with retrievalMicrosoft brought the vessel back to the surface and examined the equipment after two years on the seabed. The company reported that the underwater servers had performed more reliably than the land-based control group. InformationWeek reported that the vessel contained 864 servers and that the unit was retrieved after two years, and also noted that the servers had been installed in 12 racks and that the cooling system used cold seawater to remove heat from the equipment.Project Natick was a research program examining whether subsea facilities could be deployed close to coastal population centers, where demand for data services is concentrated. Microsoft also used the module's computing capacity for research during the COVID-19 pandemic, and its Project Natick results say the system supported Folding@home and World Community Grid after the pandemic began.The company ultimately removed the hardware and planned to recycle the pressure vessel and other components, and Microsoft's current project page says the seabed is being restored to the condition it was in before deployment.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A Naples waterfront estate returns to the market at $195 million after a $100 million price cut; why one of America’s most expensive homes still hasn’t found a buyer
articles.summary: News News: A home once listed for a staggering $295 million is back on the market in Naples, Florida, but at a dramatically lower price. Gordon Pointe, the spraw.
articles.body: A home once listed for a staggering $295 million is back on the market in Naples, Florida, but at a dramatically lower price. Gordon Pointe, the sprawling waterfront estate in the exclusive Port Royal neighbourhood, is now asking $195 million after being reduced and reshaped into a 5.39-acre offering. Realtor.com, which reported the latest listing, described the property as an iconic waterfront estate returning to the market after a $100 million price cut. Despite its extraordinary location, scale and private harbour, the estate has yet to find a buyer.From a $1 million purchase to a $295 million listingGordon Pointe has a remarkable history. Financier John Donahue began assembling the property in 1985, when he bought his first roughly four-acre waterfront parcel for about $1 million. Over the years, he expanded the family's holdings, eventually creating a much larger private compound. By 2024, the property had grown into a roughly nine-acre estate with multiple residences and extensive waterfront access. It was then placed on the market for $295 million, making it the most expensive home listing in the US at the time.The asking price reflected something that is almost impossible to recreate in Naples: an enormous private waterfront tract in one of the city's most desirable neighbourhoods. The property offers views of Naples Bay and the Gulf of Mexico, along with substantial beach frontage and a private yacht basin. Its scale and location were central to the sellers' argument that Gordon Pointe deserved a price far above that of a conventional luxury mansion.Why the property is now asking $195 millionThe estate's latest appearance on the market is somewhat different from its original offering. According to Realtor.com, Gordon Pointe has been reduced to a 5.39-acre property and is now listed for $195 million. It had most recently been offered for $210 million in January 2025 before returning to the market at the new price. Current property records show the listing at 100 & 104 Bay Road in Naples. The offering includes about 722 feet of beach frontage and a 231-foot yacht basin, with access to Naples Bay and views towards the Gulf.The reduction from $295 million to $195 million represents a $100 million drop, or roughly 34% from the original asking price. That does not mean the estate has suddenly become an ordinary luxury property. At $195 million, it remains one of the most expensive homes available in the country.What makes Gordon Pointe so valuable?For an ultra-wealthy buyer, the appeal is less about simply owning a large house and more about owning an irreplaceable piece of waterfront land. The property sits at the southern end of Gordon Drive in Port Royal. It combines privacy, direct beach frontage, boating access and views over both the bay and Gulf. The current listing describes the property as offering a protected harbour option through its yacht basin.The estate also has a history few properties can match. The Donahue family gradually assembled the land over decades, turning what began as a modest coastal property into a private compound. That history helps explain why the original asking price was so ambitious. Building a large mansion is possible; recreating a multi-acre waterfront holding in an established part of Naples is considerably harder.The hidden challenge: Florida's climate riskBut Gordon Pointe's extraordinary location also creates one of its biggest potential drawbacks. The property sits directly on the coast, making it exposed to hurricanes, storm surge and flooding. When the estate was still being offered for $295 million, flood-risk analysis by the First Street Foundation estimated a 68% chance of flooding within 15 years and 95% within 30 years. Climate-risk researchers also classified its exposure to wind as extreme.For most homeowners, those figures would be a major consideration. At the level of wealth required to purchase a $195 million property, the calculation can be different, but insurance and long-term maintenance can still become significant costs.Why hasn't someone bought it?The biggest obstacle may simply be the extremely small pool of people capable of purchasing it. At $195 million, Gordon Pointe is not competing with typical Naples homes. It is competing for the attention of a tiny group of ultra-high-net-worth buyers who want a very specific combination of privacy, waterfront access, land and prestige. The property also illustrates the difficulty of pricing trophy real estate. A seller can reduce an asking price by $100 million and still be left with a property that costs nearly $200 million.For the right buyer, however, that dramatic reduction could make Gordon Pointe considerably more compelling than it was when it carried a $295 million price tag. At $195 million, the estate remains an exceptionally rare waterfront property, offering a combination of land, privacy, beach frontage and boating access that is difficult to replicate in Naples. Whether that combination will be enough to attract a buyer remains to be seen.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? Build Your Legacy with TOI Homes.

articles.title: 'Bin Laden determined to strike in US': Declassified CIA docs reveal warnings before 9/11
articles.summary: US News: Newly declassified documents by the CIA suggest that they had repeatedly warned of possible attacks on US soil, including the possibility of an explos.
articles.body: Newly declassified documents by the CIA suggest that they had repeatedly warned of possible attacks on US soil, including the possibility of an explosive-packed aircraft being flown into a US city, years before the September 11 attacks.The CIA on Friday released 71 intelligence reports prepared for the President's Daily Brief in the years before and immediately after the 9/11 attacks, offering a detailed chronology of what US intelligence knew about Osama bin Laden and al-Qaida as their threat evolved.The collection, released as the US marked 25 years since the attacks, contains assessments dating from 1998 through September 12, 2001. While many passages remain redacted, the documents show that warnings about attacks inside the US, aircraft hijackings, Bin Laden's interest in unconventional weapons and the capabilities of his network appeared repeatedly in intelligence reports.Multiple warningsOn September 10, 1998, a CIA assessment said Bin Laden's “preferred option” was to strike the US on its own soil in Washington. It also said the same group responsible for the bombings of US embassies in Africa “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city”.The assessment cautioned, however, that intelligence provided no conclusive information about Bin Laden's intentions for future attacks.The warning was not an isolated one.A July 1998 intelligence report said Bin Laden was considering attacks in the US and noted that some of his followers had indicated a desire to bring the conflict to American soil.By December that year, another CIA assessment said Bin Laden and his allies were preparing attacks in the US, including a possible aircraft hijacking. It noted that members of the network had received hijacking training, although no group directly tied to al-Qaida had previously carried out an aircraft hijacking.The reports also tracked Bin Laden's ambitions beyond conventional attacks. An assessment from February 1998 said he and other Islamic extremists had agreed to procure chemical, biological and nuclear substances from open markets, while noting that his financial network could assist such efforts.At the same time, the CIA was following the relationship between Bin Laden and Afghanistan's Taliban rulers. A 1998 assessment said Taliban leader Mullah Omar defended Bin Laden's continued presence in Afghanistan despite pressure to rein him in, while the Taliban's dependence on narcotics revenues and financial support from Bin Laden complicated efforts to isolate him.A July 2001 report said a Bin Laden operation expected to be imminent had been postponed, but preparations for other attacks could still be underway. By August 28, a CIA assessment described al-Qaida's operations as flexible and difficult to detect, noting that cells could choose their own timing and targets and that the organisation's compartmentalised structure could limit what its leadership communicated.The August 6, 2001 President's Daily Brief, titled “Bin Laden Determined To Strike in US”, was also among the documents released. The report had previously been declassified in 2004 following a request from the 9/11 Commission.But the documents also illustrate the difficulty of turning individual warnings into a precise picture of the attack that was coming.The CIA was tracking multiple possible targets, attack plans and pieces of intelligence at the same time. In the months before 9/11, reports covered threats across several countries and regions, while separate assessments followed Bin Laden's network, the Taliban, possible attacks in the US and the group's operational capabilities.Post-attack reportThe first post-attack report, prepared at 4am on September 12, 2001, offered an early assessment of what had happened.It said mounting evidence indicated that Sunni extremists in Afghanistan and the Persian Gulf had recently been aware that Bin Laden-directed attacks were imminent. It also reported that Bin Laden had told Mullah Omar that he had operations in progress that would cause great damage to the US. One source said the attacks were the result of two years of planning and suggested the Capitol and White House may also have been targets.The release also includes reports covering the Taliban's response, the international military reaction, the shutdown of civil aviation and the impact of the attacks on financial markets in the first hours after the strikes.Taken together, the documents provide a chronological record of a threat that was repeatedly visible to US intelligence but appeared in fragments: a possible attack on US soil, aircraft hijacking, unconventional weapons, overseas operations and a highly adaptable terrorist network.The 9/11 Commission later concluded that the failure to prevent the attacks involved failures of imagination, policy, capabilities and management, with the most important being a failure of imagination.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Fighting re-erupts in Yemen and civilians are paying the price
articles.summary: More than 900 people have been killed or injured and at least 5,000 families have fled their homes in less than a week.
articles.body:
Taiz, Yemen – Aman Murshed, a mother of five in her 50s, has spent more than five years displaced in a camp in Taiz’s al-Kadaha area, hoping to return to her home where her family farmed and raised livestock.

Those dreams were vanquished when battles between the Houthis and the internationally recognised government re-erupted this month with the fiercest fighting in years.

The Houthis’ capture of the entire Red Sea coast on Friday meant that displacement “is alarmingly rising by the hour”, according to the United Nations.

“We used to hope to return home, but today we just hope to retrieve the basic belongings we left behind in the previous camp. Here we have no food and rely on neighbours to share a meal or two with us each day. I had to leave all our food behind,” Murshed told Al Jazeera English.

“The last four years were calm, and our hopes of returning home grew stronger. But suddenly, fighting erupted near our camp three days ago, and we found ourselves fleeing again toward an unknown destination.

“The only priority was to carry the children and flee as quickly as possible, because any delay could mean death. It was around 5am, and there were no cars in the camp or the surrounding area since it is on the front line. So, we walked for more than two kilometres until we found a pick-up truck that brought us to this camp for free.”

Hundreds of other families from the camp fled in every direction, some taken in by relatives or friends, while others searched for another camp that might have space for them. Many without a home now spend their days under the shade of trees, attempting to avoid the worst of the baking midday heat.

Murshed ended up at the al-Malika camp in al-Maafer district, Taiz, where she knew relatives, but her family lacks proper shelter. “They understand our suffering and will help us settle down,” she said.

The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that at least 46,000 people in Yemen have fled their homes since new clashes erupted last week.

On Friday, the Houthis captured Mocha and the last remaining parts of the Red Sea coast not under their control, sending panic through government-controlled areas and causing mass displacement.

Murshed only had time to grab a few blankets and mattresses before she fled her tent, leaving most of her belongings behind. She is most distressed about abandoning her livestock, her primary source of income and security.

“During my previous displacement, I managed to take my livestock with me. But this time, I had to leave them behind, and I am certain they were killed in the fighting.”

She is now trying to piece together a basic shelter from wooden poles and a tarpaulin donated by her neighbours, knowing that her future now lies in the hands of locals and aid groups who might help support her family.

“We used to hope to return home, but today we just hope to retrieve the basic belongings we left behind in the previous camp. Here we have no food and rely on neighbours to share a meal or two with us each day. I had to leave all our food behind,” she said.

Murshed says she can endure life without enough food and few belongings but her heart breaks for the children in the camp, who have no education, proper nutrition or other essential support.

An estimated 22.3 million people of a total population of about 35 million require humanitarian assistance and protection services in Yemen, according to the 2026 Yemen Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP) by OCHA’s ReliefWeb. These include 5.2 million internally displaced people (IDPs).

Ahmed Abduljaleel, a displaced man in his 40s living in al-Ghazaliya camp in al-Maafer district, fled his previous home in a camp in Jabal Habashi district early on Friday morning.

His story closely mirrors that of Murshed and the thousands of other families displaced by the latest fighting who had been living for years off aid.

“Our suffering is clear, but humanitarian organisations have not reached us yet to see that only women and children are sleeping under plastic sheets and using bathrooms, while men sleep outdoors. We all share the pain of a severe food shortage,” he told Al Jazeera.

Abdulnasser al-Sourouri, the branch manager in al-Maafer for the Peace and Social Security Organisation – a local nongovernmental group providing displaced people with food and essential supplies – said the ongoing fighting is piling immense pressure on aid workers who were already struggling with severe budget shortfalls before the new wave of displacements began.

“Displaced families need all basic services, including food, shelter, clean water and hygiene kits, but we lack the funds to assist everyone,” he told Al Jazeera.

“We managed to help some with shelter, but the need is vast. International organisations and the UN must intervene as soon as possible.”

Some of the fiercest fighting in previous days has been in al-Jawf, Marib and al-Bayda governorates, triggering further displacement in all three regions.

Ali Qaid, director-general of the Executive Unit for IDP Camp Management in Taiz, said that most of the displaced people had fled to al-Maafer district amid the critical security situation.

“Hundreds of families are crammed into narrow tents or right beside them, as these camps lack the capacity to absorb thousands of additional families,” Qaid told Al Jazeera.

While coordination with aid groups is under way for an urgent response to the situation, current humanitarian interventions remain weak.

Muneer, a man in his 40s who preferred to use only his first name, fled Jabal Habashi district on Friday night, leaving behind everything he owns. He was also hit by a bullet in the latest clashes.

“I was fleeing my home, following other families, when fighting suddenly broke out and I was injured in my left leg,” Muneer told Al Jazeera.

“The clashes were fierce, but praise be to Allah, it was a miracle that I made it out alive.”

Muneer has since been discharged from hospital but now relies on a cane to walk.

“We are exhausted by this war. All we want now is an end to the fighting so we can resume our normal lives,” he said.

The UN-brokered truce agreement in April 2022 had brought a temporary halt to major fighting between government-aligned forces and the Houthis, who captured the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014.

While there were periodic clashes during this period amid increased regional and maritime conflicts, this month’s fighting is the fiercest in years.

During this period, attention was focused on the Red Sea, with the Houthis targeting several ships passing Yemen during the war on Gaza, prompting US and United Kingdom air strikes on the group’s positions.

In July 2026, during the war on Iran, the Houthis threatened to attack Saudi-linked vessels passing through the Red Sea. Several ships in these waters and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia have been targeted.

Mohammed Ali, a journalist in Taiz, said Yemenis hoping for better conditions during the quieter years have been left bitterly disappointed by the reigniting of the war.

“We believed a peaceful resolution was drawing closer over the last four years, as the military fronts were quiet and there were multiple rounds of discussions between the warring parties,” Ali told Al Jazeera.

“However, the broader US-Iran conflict effectively brought an end to the 2022 truce, as the Houthis have been attempting to advance to take control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait to serve Iran’s agenda,” he said.

“The warring sides are escalating, but it is civilians who pay the price. A single visit to one of the camps for displaced families is enough to see the severe toll this escalation has taken on the Yemeni people.”

articles.title: ‘Working on Iran’s NDB membership’: Araghchi reveals Brics bank push, calls Modi-Pezeshkian meet ‘strong’
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Iran has stepped up its bid to join the New Development Bank (NDB), with foreign minister Abbas Araghchi saying Tehran has secured support .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Iran has stepped up its bid to join the New Development Bank (NDB), with foreign minister Abbas Araghchi saying Tehran has secured support from some countries and is now working to complete the requirements for membership.Araghchi, who is in New Delhi for the 18th Brics Summit, also described Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian’s meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi as a “strong”, while highlighting Iran’s expanding engagement with Brics members and other countries.Speaking to Iranian news outlet SNN Iran on Saturday, Araghchi said Tehran was actively pursuing membership of the NDB.“We are working on that today, and some countries are supportive, and they are in the process of fulfilling the necessary requirements,” he said.Iran’s bid to join the NDB was announced last month by Central Bank of Iran governor Abdolnaser Hemmati, according to TV Brics, which cited Iranian media reports.Araghchi also highlighted discussions among Brics leaders on greater use of national currencies, on Friday. Referring to the meetings, he said, “Mr Putin, Mr Modi, and Dr Pezeshkian, especially regarding the use of local currencies and national currencies, had a conversation that caught the attention of the world and attracted a lot of news coverage.”He said Saturday’s main summit would be accompanied by a series of bilateral meetings involving Pezeshkian.“Today, the main session of the summit will begin. Along with that, the President had bilateral meetings. Yesterday, there was a very strong meeting with India; today with Malaysia as well, and with Ethiopia, which is an important country in Africa,” Araghchi said.“Bilateral issues are being raised, regional issues are being raised, and praise be to God, the Islamic Republic of Iran's relations are expanding with the collection of Islamic countries and the countries of the region, and this is evident in all the meetings,” he added.Pezeshkian also used his meetings in New Delhi to push for closer economic cooperation within Brics. During his meeting with Ethiopian prime minister Abiy Ahmed Ali, he called for stronger economic and financial ties among Brics member countries and said the US presence in West Asia was a factor contributing to bloodshed.In his meeting with Malaysian prime minister Anwar Ibrahim, Pezeshkian said the region did not need a “policeman” and argued that Middle East security should be ensured by countries in the region. He also said Iran would seek to strengthen and rationalise its relations with Muslim and neighbouring countries, while emphasising that Iran is a peace-seeking country.Earlier on Friday, PM Modi also held a bilateral meeting with the Iranian president, continuing discussions from their meeting on the sidelines of the SCO Summit in Bishkek.According to the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), the two leaders reviewed various aspects of India-Iran ties, with PM Modi thanking Iran for its regular, high-level participation in Brics-related meetings despite challenging circumstances.PM Modi also thanked Pezeshkian for participating in the Leaders’ Session of the Brics Business Forum and highlighted the grouping’s potential to build “resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability” among countries of the Global South.The two leaders also discussed the conflict in West Asia. PM Modi reiterated India’s position that all issues should be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy, while stressing the need for continued efforts towards lasting peace and stability, including freedom of navigation and commerce and the safety of seafarers.In a post on X, PM Modi described the meeting as a continuation of their discussions in Bishkek.“From Bishkek to Delhi, the productive discussions continue. articles.title: Every winter, West Virginia collects families’ discarded Christmas trees and sinks them in state lakes; the branches replace woody cover used by young fish
articles.summary: US News: Discover how West Virginia turns discarded Christmas trees into vital underwater habitats for fish, addressing habitat shortages in state reservoirs through an eco-friendly recycling program.
articles.body: The Christmas tree that once stood in a family's living room does not always end its life at the kerbside in West Virginia. After the holiday season, real trees collected through the state's recycling programme can be taken to lakes and submerged, where their branches become part of an underwater landscape used by fish. What looks like a simple disposal problem on land becomes a habitat shortage being addressed beneath the surface.According to the North American Journal of Fisheries Management, the state has partnered with the West Virginia Division of Natural Resources to recycle used Christmas trees as fish habitat in lakes. The programme has operated through annual collection events, including public drop-offs at Charleston's Capitol Market, where residents have been asked to bring real trees with lights and decorations removed. Earlier state records show that more than 500 trees were collected at one event and later placed in selected lakes to provide structures where fish could hide and find food.Why the trees are neededOne reason the structures are needed is that many West Virginia reservoirs were built by damming rivers. Compared with natural lakes, reservoirs created by damming rivers can lack complex woody structure underwater. Vegetation that once grew there was cleared before flooding, leaving parts of the lake bottom without structure that could shelter small fish. In this context, a Christmas tree becomes more than recycled waste. According to the West Virginia DNR, its reservoirs often lack complex woody structure, and submerged trees can provide refuges for younger fish while also serving as ambush points for older fish.How a Christmas tree becomes fish habitatThe process is more deliberate than simply tossing a tree into a lake. An unsecured tree could be moved by currents or heavy rainfall, so fisheries biologists secure the trees before submerging them. The DNR says crews place the trunk through a cinder block and secure it with nails and boards. Once lowered into the water, the weight anchors the tree so that its branches remain upright and form a three-dimensional shelter.The resulting structure creates a maze of branches and spaces where smaller fish can take refuge. It can also provide surfaces for aquatic organisms to colonise, adding another layer to the habitat around the tree. Research published in Hydrobiologia found that fish used structurally complex littoral habitats more than unstructured areas, while experimentally added deadwood brush piles provided suitable microhabitats for several fish species. The study also found that the use of these structures varied with season and species, showing why the physical complexity of underwater habitat matters.Research published in the North American Journal of Fisheries Management has also examined the use of artificial habitat structures, including bundles of conifer branches such as discarded Christmas trees, in reservoirs. These structures can provide extra cover for fish and create areas where fish gather, making them useful tools for fisheries management. However, attracting fish to a particular location does not necessarily mean that the overall fish population has increased. West Virginia has used discarded Christmas trees in reservoirs for this purpose, giving the trees a second life while creating additional habitat for fish. From holiday decoration to long-term habitatThe practice has continued beyond individual Christmas-tree recycling events. In its fiscal 2025 annual report, the West Virginia DNR said fisheries staff deployed 1,341 habitat structures across eight impoundments, including 1,131 recycled Christmas trees. Trees were placed at Beech Fork, Burnsville, East Lynn, Mount Storm, Summersville and Tygart lakes. The agency said the structures were installed in coves, points, drop-offs, littoral areas and shoreline fishing areas that lacked sufficient habitat.This has made the program part of a broader strategy for managing artificial reservoirs. The trees do not remain whole forever, and there is a need to place them and secure them appropriately. However, when the trees remain intact, their branches can make open areas of the lakebed more complex, giving smaller fish places to hide from predators and larger fish places to hunt. It also reduces waste by giving real Christmas trees a use before they break down underwater. The practice links two very different times of year. A tree that decorated a home in December later ends up underwater. For donors, the trees become part of fish habitat in West Virginia waters rather than holiday waste.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Indian man jailed 27 years in Australia for fatal stabbing, faces deportation
articles.summary: Rest of World News: An Indian-origin man, Robin Robin, has been sentenced to 27 years in prison in Australia for the fatal stabbing of fellow student Navjeet Singh Sandhu during a drunken argument, with implications of deportation after his release.
articles.body: A 30-year-old Indian-origin man has been jailed for 27 years in Australia for fatally stabbing a fellow international student and attempting to kill another after a drunken argument in Melbourne.Robin Robin was sentenced in the Victorian Supreme Court on Friday for murdering 22-year-old Navjeet Singh Sandhu and attempting to murder 30-year-old Sharwan Singh in Ormond in May 2024, Australia Today reported.A jury found Robin guilty after he argued during the trial that he had acted in self-defence. The court imposed a 20-year non-parole period.The violence began after Robin had been drinking whisky with friends at his home while celebrating his brother Abhijeet Abhijeet buying a car. Sharwan later left the gathering to play cards at Navjeet’s home without saying goodbye, prompting Robin to call and abuse him and demand that he return repeatedly.When Sharwan eventually came back with Navjeet to collect his belongings, Robin attacked him with a knife, stabbing him in the chest.Navjeet stepped in to help his friend but was then attacked himself. Robin grabbed him by the collar and stabbed him repeatedly as he tried to get away.Navjeet suffered fatal injuries to his heart and lungs and died. Sharwan survived.Justice Andrew Tinney described the attack as “unprovoked and uncalled for” and said Robin had acted with “murderous anger”. He also described the violence as “extreme and wanton”, noting that the attack was carried out against innocent victims in a public setting and had caused fear in the community, as per the outlet.The judge also found that Robin had not demonstrated genuine remorse. After the attack, Robin fled Victoria with his brother and was arrested in New South Wales two days later.“Your lack of regret and remorse for your offending has persisted until the present time,” Justice Tinney said.Navjeet’s father, Jitender Sandhu, watched the sentencing through a video link and said his son’s death had destroyed the hopes and dreams of the family.Robin has spent more than two years behind bars since his arrest and is expected to face deportation to India after completing his prison sentence.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Four arrested during gangland violence 'day of action'
articles.summary: Police executed warrants at addresses in Bellshill and Motherwell on Friday and also recovered four stolen vehicles.
articles.body:
Police have arrested four men during a pre-planned "day of action" as part of an ongoing investigation into gangland violence.

Police executed warrants at addresses in Bellshill and Motherwell on Friday and also recovered four stolen vehicles.

One of the men arrested, a 29-year-old, was charged after a car crashed into a house in Eaglesham on Friday 21 August. There were no reports of any injuries. He is due to appear in court on Monday.

It brings the total number of arrests as part of Operation Portaledge to 81.

He was due to appear at Glasgow Sheriff Court on Friday.

A second 21-year-old man was also arrested and charged in connection with the wilful fireraising on Saturday 22 August.

A 29-year-old man was arrested and charged after a vehicle struck a property in Low Borland Way, Eaglesham on Friday 21 August. There were no reports of any injuries.

He is also due to appear in court on Monday.

A 31-year-old man was arrested and charged in connection with a wilful fire-raising of a car in Crowhill Street, Glasgow at about 04:30 on Monday 6 April. No-one was injured.

Det Ch Insp David Lamont said: "This day of action should send a clear message to those involved in this type of criminality, that we will not give up and you will be brought to justice.

"These incidents had the potential to have much more serious consequences, and I want to be absolutely clear- this type of behaviour will not be tolerated.

"Significant inquiries remain ongoing in relation to all of these incidents and we will continue to draw on detectives and specialist resources to identify anyone else involved."

In July, Police Scotland announced that an ongoing gang feud across central Scotland had come to an end.

articles.title: Ministry of Defence denies military jet caused air traffic failure
articles.summary: The glitch caused some 2,000 flight cancellations across major UK airports earlier this week.
articles.body:
The Ministry of Defence has denied a report that a military aircraft was to blame for an air traffic control system failure that caused widespread travel chaos earlier this week.

A flight plan submitted by a British military aircraft caused the outage, which led to the cancellation of more than 2,000 flights, the Financial Times reported on Friday , citing sources familiar with the incident.

The data entry caused a glitch in the system operated by National Air Traffic Services (Nats) on Tuesday, which took hours to restart, according to the newspaper.

A Ministry of Defence (MoD) spokesperson said: "We do not believe there's any indication of an error on the part of the military.

"Because it's subject to a live Nats investigation, which is expected to conclude next week, it would be inappropriate for us to comment any further while that investigation is ongoing."

A spokesperson for Nats - in which the government has a controlling interest - said it was still investigating the cause of the glitch and that it "would be wrong to speculate while that work continues".

Hundreds of thousands of people are thought to have been affected across two days of end-of-summer travel chaos after the system went down for four hours on Tuesday.

Flights in and out of the UK's main airports were affected, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Glasgow.

While Nats is expected to report back on its own investigation on Wednesday, Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander has also ordered an independent probe by the Civil Aviation Authority.

The watchdog said earlier this week that passengers were unlikely to be entitled to compensation after would-be travellers told the BBC of nightmare delays and waylaid holiday plans .

Airlines are not necessarily liable to compensate passengers for disruption caused by air traffic control.

After meeting the head of Nats, Alexander said a cyber-attack could be ruled out but added: "I do not believe this issue was unavoidable."

Nats has apologised for its third major technical fault in three years, after a computer shutdown over the August bank holiday caused travel chaos for 700,000 people in 2023 and smaller outage in 2025 caused 150 flight cancellations.

Nats is a public-private partnership, with the government holding the controlling stake of 49%. The rest is split between a group of UK airlines including BA, easyJet and Virgin Atlantic, as well as Heathrow and Nats staff.

articles.title: Brics Summit 2026: PM Modi pitches emergency support network for safety of seafarers
articles.summary: India News: The safety of Indian seafarers has emerged as a recurring focus of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Brics engagements. On Saturday, he proposed a seafar.
articles.body: The safety of Indian seafarers has emerged as a recurring focus of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Brics engagements. On Saturday, he proposed a seafarers emergency support network among BRICS members to provide distress alerts, medical aid, family communication and evacuation support.The proposal came on the opening day of the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi, where the safety and wellbeing of seafarers emerged as a recurring theme in PM Modi’s remarks amid heightened tensions in West Asia and disruptions to key shipping routes.“Seafarers make a significant contribution to global trade, but they often find themselves without adequate support during difficult times. My proposal is: Can we create a Seafarers Emergency Support Network?”, PM Modi said during his opening remarks while addressing the summit.“Through this, the Maritime Authorities and Missions of the concerned countries can be connected. It can provide support for distress alerts, medical assistance, informing families and evacuation,” he added.Modi’s proposal follows his remarks at the Brics Business Forum on Friday, when he highlighted the importance of safe sea lanes and the protection of seafarers, particularly amid the conflict in West Asia.“Global trade can move forward only when sea lanes are secure, supply routes remain open, and seafarers are safe. That is why India is a staunch advocate of freedom of navigation and the safety of seafarers,” PM Modi said at the forum.The issue also featured in PM Modi’s meeting with Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday. According to the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), PM underscored the need to ensure “freedom of navigation and commerce, and the safety and well-being of seafarers” during discussions on the conflict in West Asia.The concern has a direct bearing on India, which has a large seafaring workforce and has faced casualties amid the wider regional conflict. In July, the government had said in Parliament that 16 Indian nationals, including 10 seafarers, have lost their lives in the region since the outbreak of the of the conflict, while 75 have been injured.The summit is taking place against the backdrop of continuing geopolitical and economic uncertainty, including the West Asia crisis, disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz, the Russia-Ukraine war and US trade and tariff policies. India has repeatedly stressed the importance of keeping shipping and commercial routes open.On Saturday, PM Modi also linked the maritime proposal to a wider call for Brics to translate its consensus into practical outcomes as the grouping marked two decades since its formation.“I am delighted to welcome you all to India. India’s chairship is based on a people-centric and humanity-first approach. Resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability have been our priority,” PM Modi said.He said India had organised more than 350 meetings across nearly 30 cities during its chairship and thanked member countries for their participation.“This year's Brics summit marks a historic milestone. We are celebrating the 20th anniversary of Brics. In human life, the age of twenty heralds the beginning of a new phase of maturity and responsibility,” PM said.“This is the stage where responsibility aligns with aspirations, and potential finds a new direction. Today, Brics, too, is at a moment of coming of age,” he added.“Now is the time for us to translate the unity and consensus within Brics into tangible outcomes on the global stage.”The summit was attended by Chinese president Xi Jinping, Russian president Vladimir Putin, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince, South African president Cyril Ramaphosa, Egyptian president Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Ethiopian prime minister Abiy Ahmed Ali, Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian, Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and Indonesian president Prabowo Subianto, among other leaders and representatives.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 160-year-old St. Louis church went through a fire, 37 service requests and 2 structural condemnations; after a year-long legal fight, a neighbourhood group has won control to rehabilitate it
articles.summary: US News: For years, a 160-year-old church in St. Louis stood as a reminder of a neighbourhood’s past while steadily becoming one of its most troubled propertie.
articles.body: For years, a 160-year-old church in St. Louis stood as a reminder of a neighbourhood’s past while steadily becoming one of its most troubled properties. The vacant structure had endured a fire, repeated complaints and two structural condemnations. City records showed 37 service requests connected to the property, as concerns about its condition continued to grow. Now, after a year-long legal fight, the historic building has a new chance at survival.The Soulard Restoration Group, a neighbourhood association in St. Louis, has secured temporary possession of the vacant church through a court order, clearing the way for efforts to determine whether the deteriorating structure can be rehabilitated rather than demolished. The St. Louis Receivership Group will fund and manage the rehabilitation work.The development marks a major shift for the property, which had become a long-running concern for residents of the historic Soulard neighbourhood.From historic landmark to abandoned propertyThe church, built in 1866, is one of the older structures associated with the neighborhood's religious and architectural history. But its age eventually became part of the problem as the vacant building deteriorated.The property has an appraised value of only $23,400, according to records cited by the St. Louis Business Journal. At the same time, the building generated a long list of concerns for the city, including 37 service requests and two structural condemnations.A fire added another chapter to the building's decline. Local reports have previously described a church near Allen Avenue and South 13th Street in Soulard that burned in 2023 and remained closed afterwards. The abandoned structure became part of a wider preservation concern in the neighbourhood, where residents have repeatedly pushed for historic buildings to be repaired rather than allowed to deteriorate to the point of demolition.For the Soulard Restoration Group, the church became more than an isolated vacant building. The organisation had identified 1222 Allen Avenue, described in its November 2024 meeting minutes as “the church on Gravois,” as the first property under its new “Propertunities” initiative. The program was created to focus attention on vacant or nuisance properties and work with the city to find solutions. The group specifically said it wanted to support the city in keeping and rebuilding the structure instead of demolishing it.A legal battle over the building’s futureThat effort eventually moved from neighbourhood advocacy into court. The Soulard Restoration Group sued the church's owner in 2025, seeking to address what it described as years of deterioration. The case became a test of whether the historic structure could be rescued through a court-appointed receivership process rather than left to deteriorate further.A year later, the neighbourhood group has won a significant step in that fight. The court order gives the Soulard Restoration Group temporary possession of the property, allowing rehabilitation efforts to move forward. The arrangement is designed to give the building a chance to be stabilised and assessed rather than leaving it in limbo.The rehabilitation will be funded and managed by the St. Louis Receivership Group, according to the latest report. That distinction is important because gaining control of an abandoned historic building is only the first step. Stabilising an old structure that has suffered years of neglect, along with fire damage and structural problems, can require extensive work and significant funding.Why the neighbourhood wants to save itFor residents, the fight is about more than preserving an old building. Soulard is one of St. Louis's historic neighbourhoods, known for its rows of historic homes, brick architecture and buildings that reflect the city's immigrant and industrial past. The neighbourhood association, founded in 1972, describes its mission as building the community while preserving its heritage.The church sits within that historic landscape. The group's interest in the property also reflects a broader concern over what happens when old buildings are left vacant. Once a structure becomes severely deteriorated, the choices can become increasingly limited: spend heavily to stabilise it or eventually demolish it.The 1222 Allen Avenue property had already become a concern for the Soulard Restoration Group before the current court fight. Its 2024 meeting minutes show that the organisation was actively working with the city over the church and wanted to see the building rebuilt rather than demolished.The group’s latest victory therefore represents the culmination of a campaign that began with neighbourhood-level concern and eventually turned into a legal effort.What happens nextThe immediate priority is rehabilitation. With temporary possession secured, the property can now move into the next phase, where its condition can be evaluated and work can begin under the receivership arrangement. The objective is not simply to secure the building but to determine whether its historic fabric can be preserved and the structure returned to productive use.The road ahead is still likely to be complicated. The church has already experienced fire damage, years of vacancy and structural problems serious enough to result in two condemnations. The 37 service requests associated with the property illustrate how long the problems have persisted.But for now, demolition is no longer the only story surrounding the 160-year-old structure.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday called for a reset of global governance, saying the Global South is at the \"front row\" of global c.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday called for a reset of global governance, saying the Global South is at the "front row" of global crises but remains at the "back row" of decision-making, and urged Brics countries to replace the existing "pyramid of privilege" with a "platform of partnership".Delivering the opening remarks, as the Brics summit was officially declared open, PM Modi proposed that member countries jointly formulate 10 proposals for global governance reforms and develop them into a BRICS reform roadmap by the next summit."Today, the Global South stands in the front row of global crises but in the back row of decision-making. We must transform this 'pyramid of privilege' into a 'platform of partnership' -- one where every nation has a voice, every member has a stake, and the development of humanity lies at the heart of every effort," PM said."In this regard, I propose that we jointly formulate 10 proposals for global governance reform, aiming to shape them into a BRICS reform roadmap by the time of the next summit," he added.The Prime Minisyer also called for time-bound reform of global institutions, particularly the United Nations Security Council, saying its restructuring "can no longer be postponed". "In formulating this roadmap, we must focus on three key aspects: Representation, Responsiveness, and Rule-making," he said, adding that voting power, leadership positions and policy priorities in financial institutions must reflect "today's economic realities".He also proposed a Brics continuity and implementation mechanism, using the "Troika" arrangement of the previous, current and incoming chairs to track initiatives and outcomes. "This would enable the follow-up of all initiatives and outcomes through the 'Troika' arrangement. We could also create a secure digital repository to record the nodal point, timeframe, and implementation status associated with every decision."PM Modi further reiterated that Brics had established a distinct identity on the global stage and was "not against anyone". articles.title: American flight attendant reveals why you should never eat off airplane's tray tables: “Why do people do this?”
articles.summary: A Texas-based flight attendant has warned passengers about one of the dirtiest surfaces they regularly touch on a flight. She said it’s the tray table.
articles.body: A Texas-based flight attendant has warned passengers about one of the dirtiest surfaces they regularly touch on a flight. She said it’s the tray table. According to the cabin crew member, some parents change their babies’ dirty diapers on the same fold-down tables where passengers later place their food, drinks and personal belongings.Janae, a flight attendant who shares travel and workplace experiences on TikTok, spoke about the issue in a video shared with her more than 22,000 followers. She explained why she avoids eating directly from airplane tray tables and why she is cautious about touching items left on them. Her warning has drawn attention to an everyday part of flying that passengers often overlook.“People change their kids’ diapers on those tray tables”In her video, Janae said she does not eat off airplane tray tables or place her personal belongings directly on them. “People change their kids' diapers on those tray tables on airplanes; that’s why, as a flight attendant, I don’t ever eat off of those tray tables, I don’t put any of my stuff on those tray tables,” she said.The concern is that a surface used for diaper changes may later be used to hold snacks, meals or other items. Passengers may not know what happened on the tray table before they sat down. Janae also described how she protects the surface when she needs to use it.“If I have to, I take a trash bag and lay it over the surface,” she said. She added that simply wiping the table with a disinfectant wipe may not always be enough. “Even wiping it down with Lysol wipes,” she continued, “the area has to stay wet for 10 minutes for it to actually be fully effective.”Why she refuses to take dirty diapers from passengersJanae also spoke about a situation she says flight attendants encounter during flights when parents approach crew members with their child’s used diaper after changing it. “Why do people do this? Why do people change their kids’ dirty diapers on tray tables where people are going to be putting their stuff and eating? Because they don’t think,” she said.She then described what happens when passengers try to hand over the waste. “As a flight attendant, people will come up and try to hand you their dirty diapers and we’re like, ‘No! Let me get gloves at the bare minimum.’” Janae said she does not want to take the diaper even when wearing gloves, adding that some parents become offended by her refusal.“I won’t even take it with gloves but the parents act offended at that,” she said. Instead, she said she gives parents garbage bags and expects them to manage their child’s waste themselves.Flight attendant warns passengers about other dirty airplane surfacesTray tables are not the only parts of an aircraft that have been highlighted by flight attendants. Janae also criticised passengers who expect crew members to handle vomit in their barf bags, those who refuse to wash their hands after using the lavatory and travellers who walk barefoot through the cabin. Her concerns are part of a wider conversation among cabin crew about the surfaces passengers touch during a flight.Cher, a Texas-based flight attendant, previously shared warnings about some of the dirtiest areas of an Airbus. Her list included window shades, carpets, overhead bins and safety straps. Another flight attendant, Josephine Remo, separately highlighted the bathroom sink faucet and door lock as areas that passengers should be careful about touching.These warnings focus on places that may be overlooked when passengers think about airplane cleanliness.What passengers can do before eating on a flightJanae’s warning does not mean that every airplane tray table is contaminated with baby waste. Her comments describe what she says she has encountered as a flight attendant. However, passengers can take a few simple precautions:Clean the tray table before using it: Wipe the surface with a suitable disinfectant product and follow the instructions on its label.Avoid placing food directly on the table: Use a clean plate, wrapper or other suitable barrier.Wash or sanitise your hands before eating: This is especially useful after touching shared surfaces.Keep personal belongings off the tray table: Bags, phones and other items can pick up dirt from frequently touched surfaces.Dispose of diapers responsibly: Parents should use the appropriate waste-disposal arrangements rather than handing used diapers to crew members or leaving them on tray tables.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: Rafale set for major firepower boost as France fast-tracks F5 upgrade amid India’s 114-jet plan
articles.summary: News News: France has accelerated preparations for the Rafale F5, the next major upgrade of its Rafale fighter, with the country’s defence procurement agency awa.
articles.body: France has accelerated preparations for the Rafale F5, the next major upgrade of its Rafale fighter, with the country’s defence procurement agency awarding contracts for key technologies ahead of the programme’s formal development phase.According to France’s Directorate General of Armament (DGA), preparatory contracts have been awarded to Dassault Aviation, Thales, Safran and MBDA. The Rafale F5 development phase is expected to begin by the end of 2026.The upgrade is set to bring major improvements to the fighter’s radar, electronic warfare, propulsion, connectivity and weapons capabilities.Rafale F5 upgradesThe Rafale F5 is being developed as a major mid-life upgrade designed to improve the fighter’s ability to operate against increasingly sophisticated threats.One of the key changes will be the introduction of the Thales RBE2-XG radar. According to The War Zone, citing the French DGA, the radar is expected to use gallium-nitride (GaN) technology, providing greater power and detection range while improving the identification of targets with extremely low radar cross-sections.The radar will also have greater computing capacity for artificial intelligence applications and is being designed to support collaborative combat, allowing sensors to work together with reduced pilot intervention.The Rafale’s SPECTRA electronic warfare suite will also undergo a major redesign. The War Zone reports that the F5 version, being developed by MBDA and Thales, will adopt a fully digital architecture to improve threat detection and jamming capabilities.The DGA says the upgrade is intended to counter the increasing density of threats and the growing complexity of hostile radar waveforms expected by 2035.The fighter will also receive a new Inter-Vehicle Data Link (IVDL) developed by Thales. France’s DGA describes the system as a high-speed, discreet and jamming-resistant communications link.For propulsion, Safran is developing the M88 T-Rex engine. According to The War Zone, the engine is planned to increase maximum thrust from around 75 kN to nearly 90 kN, an increase of roughly 20%.The additional thrust is intended to support the Rafale F5’s more demanding sensors, electronic systems and weapons.On the weapons front, the F5 is being developed around the ASN4G, France’s future air-launched nuclear missile. The War Zone reports that the missile is expected to reach speeds above Mach 5 and have a range of more than 1,000 km, with entry into service planned around 2035.The F5 is also expected to receive a successor to the Meteor beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile.Why F5 matters for IndiaThe accelerated Rafale F5 programme comes at a significant time for India, which is preparing to substantially expand its Rafale fleet.India is planning to acquire 114 Rafale fighters under the Multi-Role Fighter Aircraft (MRFA) programme. According to reports, Dassault Aviation submitted its proposal in August 2026, with 18 aircraft to be delivered from France and the remaining 96 to be manufactured in India.The F5 upgrade could be particularly relevant to India as its new Rafales are expected to be delivered initially in the F4 standard, with a potential upgrade path to F5.If the MRFA deal goes ahead, India could eventually operate a much larger Rafale fleet while gaining access to the F5’s upgraded radar, electronic warfare systems, connectivity and propulsion, alongside future weapons being developed for the aircraft.

articles.title: Ukraine claims to have struck rubber factory in Russia
articles.summary: Ukraine says it has attacked a Russian rubber factory in the Samara region on the Volga river. A fire was detected on the premises of the plant in Togliatti,...
articles.body:
Ukraine says it has attacked a Russian rubber factory in the Samara region on the Volga river.

A fire was detected on the premises of the plant in Togliatti, the General Staff in Kiev reported on Saturday.

The company specializes in the production of synthetic rubbers, which are important for the use of tactical and ballistic missiles, according to the statement.

Early on Saturday, Russian regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev reported a major Ukrainian drone attack on Telegram, without providing details about the target.

The mayor of Togliatti, Ilya Sukhih, said that one person had been taken to hospital following a massive attack on the city. Several multi-storey residential buildings have been damaged, he said.

Unverified images and videos purporting to show a large cloud of smoke in Togliatti were circulating on social media. The city is located around 750 kilometres from Russia's border with Ukraine.

Ukraine has been defending itself against a large-scale Russian invasion for more than four and a half years with Western assistance.

As part of its defensive campaign, it repeatedly targets locations deep within Russian territory.

articles.title: Trump says Iran 'probably' behind Saudi pipeline attack as oil route shut
articles.summary: US News: US President Donald Trump on Saturday said Iran was probably responsible for an aerial attack on Saudi Arabia that forced the shutdown of the kingdom'.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Saturday said Iran was probably responsible for an aerial attack on Saudi Arabia that forced the shutdown of the kingdom's East-West oil pipeline, a key route for exporting crude while bypassing the Strait of Hormuz."I think they are, probably they are," Trump told reporters in Dublin when asked whether Iran was responsible for the attack on the vital oil conduit.Trump said he had spoken with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, whom he described as a "good friend".The MAGA president also said Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels had contacted his administration and indicated that they did not want the United States to become directly involved in the conflict."They would much prefer not having us involved, and they're letting most ships go through. There's just one country that they're not too happy with, and we'll get that straightened out," Trump said.Pipeline shut after drone attacksSaudi Arabia shut down its major East-West oil pipeline after drone attacks struck pumping stations in the Riyadh and Madinah regions on Thursday, leaving several people injured and causing damage that is still being assessed.The Saudi Energy Ministry said the pipeline was shut down as "a precautionary measure" following multiple attacks. The Saudi Foreign Ministry said several drones had entered from Iraq, where Iran-backed militias operate, and that the strikes "caused human injuries and damage."The kingdom has so far refrained from retaliating after Iraq's prime minister asked Riyadh to give Baghdad time to take action against those responsible.Saudi Arabia said it "reserves the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, its security, its facilities," and its inhabitants.Built in the 1980s, the roughly 1,200-km East-West pipeline runs from Saudi Arabia's oil-producing eastern region to Yanbu on the Red Sea coast.The pipeline has become increasingly important during the Iran war as it allows Saudi Arabia to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, where tanker traffic has been severely disrupted.The pipeline has carried between 4 million and 5 million barrels of crude a day in recent months, equivalent to around 4% to 5% of global oil supply, according to ship-tracking companies and analysts.An initial assessment by US officials found that pumping stations alongside the pipeline had been hit. Satellite imagery showed fire and thick black smoke rising from at least one pumping station, although it remained unclear how long repairs would take or whether the pipeline itself had been damaged.Saudi Arabia said it had chosen not to respond "at this stage" following the request from Iraq's prime minister.Iraq condemned the attack and said it would not allow its territory or airspace to be used to launch attacks against Saudi Arabia or neighbouring countries. Baghdad also dismissed a military commander after an investigation found that the attack originated from Iraq.Trump also said that he would "love" to see Ireland reunified with British-run Northern Ireland, saying he believed it would eventually happen."Well, I don't want to cause any problems, but I will tell you, I'd love to see it unified," Trump told reporters after meeting Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin. "The way I look at it, it's going to happen eventually ... I think it would be a fantastic thing.""Now the UK will have something to say about it ... but I think it would be a great thing," Trump added.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
